title: Are You the First Man Born?
sum: The second round of the debate opens, and Eliphaz, the oldest and gentlest of the friends, has lost patience. Job's words are only wind (15:2). Worse, they are dangerous: they undo reverence and prayer for anyone who hears them (15:4). Job's own mouth convicts him (15:6). Does he think he is the first man ever born, or that he sat in God's council (15:7–8)? The friends have the old men and the tradition of the fathers on their side, and they have offered Job God's own comfort (15:9–11). No human is clean before God, so how can Job claim to be (15:14–16)?

Then Eliphaz recites what the wise have handed down (15:17–19): a long poem on the wicked man. He lives in dread all his days, waiting for the sword (15:20–24), because he charged at God like a soldier (15:25–27). His wealth will not last; fire will dry up his branches; he is like a vine that drops its grapes and an olive that sheds its blossom (15:28–33). The godless are barren, their tents burn, and their only children are trouble and lies (15:34–35).
readings: Read as a defense of faith

Eliphaz's main fear is not that Job is wrong about himself but that he is harming religion. If a man like Job can say that God is unjust, who will keep praying (15:4)? Eliphaz defends the tradition of the fathers, the fear of God and the order of the world. His tone has hardened since chapters 4–5, but his concern is that of a pastor who sees a believer saying things that could destroy other believers' faith.
Read as the trap of a good doctrine

Eliphaz's poem on the wicked (15:20–35) is fine poetry and largely biblical: the wicked do live in fear, and evil does bring its own ruin (Psalm 7:14–16; Proverbs 28:1). But told to a man who has lost his children, his wealth and his health, it becomes an accusation. Every detail, fire on the tents, children cut off, wealth gone, matches Job's story. The doctrine is not false; its use is.
Read with the reader's knowledge

The reader knows what Eliphaz does not. He asks whether Job listened in God's council (15:8); the reader has seen that council and heard God call Job blameless (1:8; 2:3). He says no human is clean before God (15:14); God has said Job is one of a kind. The irony is the book's way of testing the friends' confidence.

views.H: Traditional readers take Eliphaz as a real elder from Teman, the Edomite town famous for wisdom, speaking for the old wisdom of the East. Many note that much of what he says is true and is repeated elsewhere in Scripture, and that his error is in applying it to Job. Some traditional readers point out that Eliphaz is the friend God addresses by name in 42:7.
views.C: Critical scholars note that the second cycle (15–21) has a clear pattern: each friend gives a poem on the fate of the wicked, and Job answers by turning away from them, to God (16–17), to his isolation and hope (19), and finally to the evidence of experience (21). Eliphaz's appeal to an unmixed tradition (15:18–19) is sometimes read as a sign of the book's setting in the Persian period, when the purity of the community was a live issue. The chapter's vocabulary is rich in rare words (15:24, 29), a mark of the poet's style.
views.W: Appeals to the wisdom of the ancestors are standard in ancient Near Eastern wisdom. The Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend, has the friend answer the sufferer's complaints by insisting that the godless will soon be cut down and that the ways of the gods are beyond knowing. The Egyptian Instruction literature also appeals to 'the sayings of the ancestors'. Eliphaz speaks as such a sage. What is new in Job is that the tradition itself is put on trial.
views.J: Maimonides reads the friends as schools of thought about providence: Eliphaz stands for the view he calls the opinion of our Law, that suffering is always deserved and comes because of sin, even if the sin is unknown (Guide 3.23). The Talmud counts Eliphaz, with Job, Bildad, Zophar and Elihu, among the seven prophets who prophesied to the nations (Bava Batra 15b), and later tradition sometimes links him with Esau's son Eliphaz, whose son was Teman (Genesis 36:10–11).
views.X: Gregory the Great reads the friends as figures of heretics who say many true things about God but mix them with error and speak them with pride; Eliphaz's harsh words to Job are like the false teachers' words to the church. Calvin preached that the friends defend a doctrine that is true in general but falsely applied, and that this is a warning to every preacher. Paul quotes Eliphaz once with approval (1 Corinthians 3:19 cites Job 5:13).

deep.h: The second round of the debate
deep.b:
The speeches of chapters 4–14 made up the first round: each friend spoke once, and Job answered each. Chapters 15–21 repeat the pattern: Eliphaz (15), Job (16–17), Bildad (18), Job (19), Zophar (20), Job (21). The tone is harsher. The friends no longer urge Job to seek God and be restored, as they did in 5:8, 8:5–7 and 11:13–19. Instead, all three describe the fate of the wicked, in poems that look more and more like a portrait of Job.

Job, for his part, almost stops arguing with them. He speaks past them, to God and about God (16:7–17), to the earth and to a witness in heaven (16:18–21), and to anyone who will write down his words (19:23–27). Only in chapter 21 does he take on their claim directly, with evidence: the wicked often live long, die at ease and are buried with honor. The round ends with Job's verdict that their answers are 'faithlessness' (21:34).

Eliphaz is not a villain. He is the most courteous of the friends; he began by praising Job for having strengthened others (4:3–4). His theology is that of much of the Bible: God is just; no human is pure before him (Psalm 143:2); the wicked bring ruin on themselves (Psalm 7:14–16); and suffering can be God's correction (5:17; Proverbs 3:11–12). He appeals to two kinds of authority, a vision (4:12–21) and the tradition of the fathers (15:17–19).

His mistake, as the book presents it, is to assume that the doctrine must explain this case. He reasons backward from Job's suffering to Job's guilt. And he treats honest protest as impiety (15:4), when God will later say that Job, not the friends, spoke rightly of him (42:7). The chapter asks the reader to hold both: a true doctrine, and the cruelty of using it as a verdict on a sufferer.

settings.what: Eliphaz's second speech: Job's words condemn him, and the wicked live in dread
settings.by: Eliphaz the Temanite, the oldest of the three friends
settings.to: Job, sitting among the ashes (2:8; outside the town in the Greek and in later tradition), with Bildad and Zophar listening
settings.when: after Job's long reply to Zophar (12–14), in which Job mocked the friends' wisdom and turned to God
settings.why: Eliphaz wants to stop Job's speech, which he sees as harmful to faith, and to warn him. He first rebukes Job's pride (15:2–16), then recites the tradition about the fate of the wicked (15:17–35), hoping Job will see himself in it before it is too late.
settings.readers: For Israelites reading after the exile, Eliphaz voiced the answer many had been taught: disaster proves sin, and the faithful must not question God. Hearing it spoken to a man the reader knows is innocent made them ask whether that answer was enough for their own suffering.
views: Eliphaz speaks out of concern for Job and for the community's faith (Andersen, Hartley).
The speech marks the friends' turn from comfort to accusation, preparing for Eliphaz's open charges in 22:5–9 (Clines, Habel).

title: My Witness Is in Heaven
sum: Job answers that he has heard enough: the friends are comforters who bring trouble (16:2). If they were in his place, he could pile up words and shake his head at them too (16:4–5). Then he turns from them to describe what God has done. God has worn him out, wrecked his household and seized him, and his wasted body has become a witness against him (16:7–8). God tore him in anger, ground his teeth at him, handed him over to the wicked. He grabbed Job by the neck, set him up as a target for his archers, and broke through him like a soldier breaching a wall (16:9–14). Job sits in sackcloth with his face raw from crying, though his hands have done no violence and his prayer is clean (16:15–17).

Then the turn. Job calls on the earth not to cover his blood, so that his cry for justice will not die (16:18). And he says that even now he has a witness in heaven, one who vouches for him on high, who will plead for a man with God as one person pleads for a friend (16:19–21). His years are few, and he is about to go on the road of no return (16:22).
readings: Read as lament

Much of chapter 16 is the language of the lament psalms: enemies gaping and striking, God as an attacker, tears and dust and sackcloth (Psalm 22:7, 13; Psalm 88; Lamentations 3). Job says what many sufferers feel but rarely say: that the enemy is God.
Read as a lawsuit

The chapter is full of legal words: witness (16:8, 19), testify (16:8), plead a case (16:21). Job's blood is like a murder victim's, crying for justice (16:18). Having no court on earth, he appeals to one in heaven. The trial he wanted in chapters 9 and 13 is taking shape in his mind.
Read as a paradox of faith

The same God who tears Job apart (16:9) is the God to whom Job weeps (16:20) and before whom his witness pleads (16:21). Job appeals from God to God. Many readers find here the deepest kind of faith: holding on to God against God, as Jacob held the one who wrestled with him (Genesis 32:26).

views.H: Traditional readers hear the cry of a real sufferer who, at his lowest point, still believes that heaven holds the truth about him. Most take the witness to be God himself, or the God Job trusts behind the God he experiences. Christian traditional readers add that the witness is fulfilled in Christ.
views.C: Critical scholars see chapter 16 as the start of a line of 'mediator' figures in Job (9:33; 16:19–21; 19:25; 33:23). Since Mowinckel (1925), many have argued that the witness is a heavenly being distinct from God, a member of the divine council who will defend Job against the Accuser's charges, a role like that of the personal god who pleads for a person in Mesopotamian religion. Others (Clines) take the witness to be Job's own cry, personified.
views.W: In Mesopotamia a person's 'personal god' was expected to intercede for him in the assembly of the gods, and suffering was often explained as that god's anger or absence. Ludlul bel nemeqi has the sufferer's god and goddess abandon him before Marduk restores him. The Sumerian 'Man and His God' has the sufferer plead with his own god. Job has no such lesser god to appeal to; if there is a heavenly advocate, he must come from the one God.
views.J: Jewish interpreters have usually understood the witness as God himself, who knows that Job's hands are free of violence (so Rashi, for example). The rabbinic idea of advocates and accusers before God (Mishnah Avot 4:11: whoever keeps one commandment gains one advocate) gives another frame for the scene.
views.X: Christian readers have read 16:19–21 as a longing fulfilled in Christ, the advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1), who intercedes for us (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25), the one mediator who is himself human, a 'son of man' (16:21; 1 Timothy 2:5). Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas both read the witness as Christ. Many modern Christian scholars hold that the text points toward this without stating it.

deep.b:
Four answers have strong defenders. God himself. Job appeals from the God who attacks him to the God who knows the truth. This is the oldest reading in Judaism and Christianity alike, and it has modern defenders (Gordis, Andersen, Hartley). It explains why the witness is 'in heaven' and why Job weeps 'to God' in the next line. Its difficulty is 16:21, which says the witness pleads 'with God', as if they are two.

A heavenly advocate. Mowinckel argued in 1925 that the witness, and the go'el of 19:25, is a heavenly being who will take Job's side, a counterpart to the Accuser of chapters 1–2 and like the 'mediating angel' Elihu describes (33:23). Pope, Habel and Newsom have developed the view. It fits 16:21 well and fits the divine council of the prologue. Its difficulty is that Job nowhere else expects any heavenly being to oppose God.

Job's own cry. Clines reads 'my witness' as the outcry of 16:18, the blood that will not be silenced, rising to heaven to testify. This fits the verse's link with 16:18 and avoids a second heavenly figure. Its difficulty is the personal language of 16:21.

Christ. Christian readers from the fathers on have seen here the advocate and intercessor of the New Testament (1 John 2:1; Hebrews 7:25). Most who hold this read it as fulfillment, not as Job's own conscious meaning.

The Old Greek translator, working perhaps in the 100s BC, softened and shortened Job's harshest lines. In 16:20 the Greek has 'may my prayer come to the Lord' in place of the Hebrew's 'my mockers are my friends'. In 16:8 Job's 'leanness' becomes his 'lie' (to pseudos mou). The Old Greek also lacked parts of 16:3, 16:8 and 16:21, which Origen filled in from Theodotion's translation (marked with an asterisk). I checked the Greek in Rahlfs and the asterisks in the NETS translation of Job, not in Ziegler's Göttingen edition.

echoes: 2:11; 6:4; 9:33; 13:24; 15:2; 15:25–26; 17:3; 19:25; 30:21; 33:23; Genesis 4:10; Isaiah 26:21; Isaiah 50:6; Isaiah 53:9; Lamentations 2:4; Lamentations 3:12–13; Psalm 22:7; Matthew 27:39; 1 John 2:1; Hebrews 7:25; Hebrews 12:24

settings.what: Job's reply to Eliphaz: God has torn me, but my witness is in heaven
settings.to: The three friends at first (16:2–6; 17:10), then God, spoken of and spoken to (16:7–17; 17:3–4), the earth (16:18), and himself
settings.when: right after Eliphaz's second speech, which called Job's words wind and described the fate of the wicked
settings.why: Job rejects the friends' comfort, describes God's assault on him as the violence of an enemy, and, having no court on earth, appeals to a witness in heaven and asks God to stand bail for him (17:3). The speech ends in despair of any hope in this life (17:11–16). Its purpose is not to persuade the friends but to keep his case alive before God.
settings.readers: Readers in the shadow of the exile, who had prayed laments like Lamentations 3 over a ruined Jerusalem, would hear in Job's words their own complaint that God had become an enemy, and a bold hope that heaven still held the truth about them.
views: Job appeals to God against God (Gordis, Andersen, Hartley).
A member of the divine council who will defend Job (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel).
His own outcry, rising to heaven (Clines).

title: Where Then Is My Hope?
sum: Job's speech goes on. His spirit is broken; his days are snuffed out; the grave is waiting (17:1). Mockers surround him (17:2). He asks God to put down a pledge for him and stand as his guarantor, since no one else will shake hands on his behalf (17:3). God has closed the friends' minds, and Job has become a byword among the peoples, a face for spitting in (17:4–7). The upright should be shocked at this, and the righteous will hold to their way (17:8–9), but among his friends Job finds no one wise (17:10).

The chapter ends in the grave. Job's days and plans are gone, though the friends keep promising that light is near (17:11–12). If all he can hope for is Sheol, a bed in the dark, with the Pit for his father and the maggot for his mother and sister, then where is his hope? Will it go down with him into the dust (17:13–16)?
readings: Read as the low point

Chapter 17 is Job at his lowest. In chapter 14 he still wished God would hide him in Sheol and remember him (14:13). Here Sheol is simply home, and hope dies with him. The darkness of this chapter is the background against which 19:25 rises.
Read as legal hope

Even here, Job uses the language of the law: pledge, surety, striking hands (17:3). He does not give up his case; he asks God to guarantee it. The despair is about this life; the appeal to God is not withdrawn.
Read with the question of resurrection

Job's question, 'Where then is my hope?' (17:15), is the question that later Jewish and Christian hope answers with the resurrection of the dead. Job himself does not give that answer here. His honesty about death without hope is one reason readers take his hope in 19:25–27 so seriously.

views.H: Traditional readers hear in 17:3 an appeal to God as the only one who could vouch for Job. Christian traditional readers often see the guarantor fulfilled in Christ, 'the guarantor of a better covenant' (Hebrews 7:22). They read 17:9, the righteous holding to their way, as Job's real faith shining through his despair.
views.C: Critical scholars note the difficulties of the Hebrew (17:2, 5, 16), and many think 17:8–10 has been disturbed or is ironic. They see the chapter as the end of a carefully built speech, moving from the friends (16:2–6) to God's assault (16:7–17), to hope in heaven (16:18–17:3), and back to despair (17:11–16), a pattern of rise and fall that Job's speeches often follow.
views.W: Mesopotamian laments also picture the underworld as a dark house of dust from which no one returns; the Descent of Ishtar describes the 'house of darkness' where the dead eat clay. Job's picture of Sheol as a dark house with beds draws on the same common imagery. But where Mesopotamian sufferers expect a god to restore them in this life (as Marduk does in Ludlul), Job here expects nothing.
views.J: Jewish commentators generally read 17:9 as Job's own statement that, despite his suffering, the righteous will not abandon God's ways. The Talmud (Bava Batra 16a) takes Job's statements about Sheol as part of the evidence that he doubted the resurrection of the dead, a verdict others in the same discussion soften.
views.X: Christian readers have used 17:9 as a text on perseverance: the righteous keep on their road, and those with clean hands grow stronger. The picture of calling the grave 'father' and the maggot 'mother' was read by the fathers as Job's humility before death. The Office of the Dead read 17:1–3 and 17:11–15 as one of its readings at night prayer for the dead, placing Job's despair beside Christian hope.

deep.b:
Job uses 'hope' (tiqvah) as a key word. Eliphaz told him his hope should be his integrity (4:6). Job said his days end without hope (7:6), that a tree has more hope than a man (14:7), that God destroys human hope (14:19). Now he asks where his hope is, if it goes down with him to Sheol (17:15–16). In 19:10 he says God has pulled it up by the roots.

Yet hope does not vanish from the book. In 13:15 Job says he will argue his case before God whatever happens. In 16:19 and 19:25 he speaks with certainty of a witness and a redeemer. The movement is not steady progress from despair to faith. It goes back and forth, as real grief does, and that is part of what makes the chapter honest.

11QtgJob, an Aramaic translation of Job found in Cave 11 at Qumran in 1956, is the oldest surviving translation of Job besides the Greek. Its first surviving column preserves parts of 17:14–18:4. In chapters 15–21 the published editions report fragments of about 17:14–18:4, 19:11–19, 19:29–20:6, 21:2–10 and 21:20–27. It shows that the book was being translated into Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the late Second Temple period, by the first century BC or AD. A rabbinic tradition says that Gamaliel the Elder ordered a Targum of Job to be buried under the Temple Mount (Bavli Shabbat 115a), which shows that such translations existed and that some rabbis were uneasy with them. I checked the coverage against the published reports, not the plates.

title: The Lamp of the Wicked Goes Out
sum: Bildad has had enough of Job's words and his insults: why does Job treat the friends like dumb animals (18:2–3)? Job is tearing himself apart in his rage, and the world will not be rearranged for him, any more than a rock will move from its place (18:4).

Then Bildad paints the fate of the wicked. His lamp goes out (18:5–6). His stride is cramped and his own scheming brings him down (18:7). He walks into traps of every kind: net, mesh, spring-trap, noose, cord, snare (18:8–10). Terrors chase him, ruin waits for him to slip, disease eats his skin, and the firstborn of Death feeds on his limbs (18:11–13). He is torn from his tent and marched to the king of terrors; sulfur is scattered on his land; his roots dry up and his branches wither (18:14–16). His name vanishes, he is driven out of the world, and he leaves no child or grandchild (18:17–19). All the world is stunned at his end. 'That is the place of one who does not know God' (18:21).
readings: Read as a portrait of Job

Bildad never names Job, but almost every line fits him: the darkened tent, the skin eaten away (2:7), the house without children (1:18–19), fire from heaven on his property (1:16), the horrified onlookers (2:12). The poem is a portrait of Job drawn as a wicked man, and Bildad's last line makes the charge: Job does not know God.
Read as wisdom poetry

Taken on its own, the poem is a fine piece of wisdom poetry, full of the hunter's language and the imagery of light, plants and memory. It teaches what Proverbs and the Psalms teach: evil traps itself, and the wicked do not last (Proverbs 5:22; Psalm 9:15–16; Psalm 37). Bildad is not inventing a doctrine; he is applying a common one.
Read as a debate

Bildad answers Job point by point. Job said God's anger tore him (16:9); Bildad says Job tears himself (18:4). Job pictured himself in a net (implied in 16:12–14); Bildad says the wicked walk into their own (18:8). Job's hope was to be remembered (14:13); Bildad says the wicked are forgotten (18:17). Job will answer back in chapter 19, and again with facts in chapter 21.

views.H: Traditional readers take Bildad as a real sage from Shuah (Genesis 25:2, a son of Abraham and Keturah), defending a true doctrine with a false application. They note that God rebukes all three friends (42:7) but that Bildad's teaching on the end of the wicked is repeated in Scripture, and so is true in its proper place.
views.C: Critical scholars admire the craft of the poem: its six words for traps, its personified Death and 'king of terrors', and its tight structure, from light (18:5–6) to traps (18:7–10) to terror and disease (18:11–14) to the end of name and line (18:15–21). Many see in the 'firstborn of Death' and 'king of terrors' traces of older Canaanite myth about Mot. Some think Bildad's speeches in the third round (25) have been cut short.
views.W: Ancient Near Eastern texts also picture the underworld as ruled by a king (Nergal in Mesopotamia; Mot in Ugaritic myth), and the dead as captives led there. Curse texts and treaty curses threaten the loss of name, seed and memory, just as Bildad does (compare the curses at the end of the Code of Hammurabi). Bildad's poem uses the shared language of curse to describe the fate of the wicked.
views.J: Maimonides assigns Bildad the view of the Mu'tazila, that suffering is a test or is balanced by reward, and that God's justice is complete when the account is closed (Guide 3.23). The Talmud names the friends among the seven prophets to the nations (Bava Batra 15b).
views.X: Gregory the Great read the friends' speeches allegorically, finding in them true descriptions of the wicked spoken by men who misapplied them. Christian readers link the 'king of terrors' with Hebrews 2:14–15, where Christ frees those held in slavery by the fear of death. Calvin's sermons on Job make the point that the friends' words were true of the wicked in general but that God's servants must not judge any one sufferer by them.

deep.b:
Set side by side, Bildad's wicked man and the Job of the prologue are disturbingly alike.

The lamp in the tent goes out (18:5–6): Job's children died in a house that fell (1:19). Skin eaten away (18:13): Job's skin is covered with sores (2:7; 7:5). Torn from the tent he relied on (18:14): Job's security is gone (3:25–26). Sulfur on his land (18:15): the fire of God burned his flocks (1:16). No child or grandchild (18:19): his ten children are dead (1:18–19). The world horrified (18:20): his friends wept and tore their robes when they saw him (2:12).

Bildad's method is to reason from the effect to the cause: since Job suffers what the wicked suffer, Job must be wicked. Job's reply in 19:6 rejects the method. The effects are real, he says, but the cause is God, who has wronged him.

settings.what: Bildad's second speech: the trap closes on the wicked
settings.to: Job (with 'you' in the plural in 18:2–3, perhaps lumping Job with those like him), before the other friends
settings.when: after Job's despairing speech of chapters 16–17, in which he called the friends unwise (17:10) and appealed to a witness in heaven
settings.why: Bildad defends the friends' honor (18:3) and the stability of the moral order (18:4), then describes the end of the wicked so vividly that Job cannot miss the resemblance. He means to frighten Job into seeing his danger, and he ends with the charge that such a man does not know God (18:21).
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, Bildad's poem was familiar wisdom, the kind of thing taught in Proverbs. Set beside the reader's knowledge of Job's innocence, it showed how a true teaching can be used to crush a righteous sufferer, and it warned them against judging the afflicted.

title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
sum: Job answers Bildad: how long will the friends crush him with words? Ten times they have shamed him (19:2–3). Even if he had erred, it would be his own affair (19:4). If they want to use his disgrace against him, let them know that it is God who has wronged him and thrown his net around him (19:5–6). He cries 'Violence!' and no one answers. God has walled his road, stripped his glory, uprooted his hope and sent his troops to besiege his tent (19:7–12).

Everyone has abandoned him: brothers, kin, friends, house guests, servant girls, his own servant, his wife, his family, children in the street, his inner circle (19:13–19). He is skin and bone, escaped with only the skin of his teeth (19:20). He begs the friends for pity, since God's hand has struck him (19:21–22).

Then Job wishes his words could be written down, carved in rock forever (19:23–24), and he makes the most famous statement in the book: 'As for me, I know that my redeemer lives, and at last he will stand up on the dust.' Even after his skin is stripped away, he will see God, with his own eyes, not as a stranger, and he longs for it with all his being (19:25–27). He ends with a warning: the friends who hunt him should fear judgment themselves (19:28–29).
readings: Read as resurrection hope

In the Greek and Latin translations, in most church fathers and in the Christian liturgy, 19:25–27 is Job's confession that he will rise from the dead and see God in his own body at the last day. Christ is the living Redeemer, and the verse is read at funerals as the hope of the faithful. On this reading, Job sees farther than anyone else in the Old Testament up to his time.
Read as vindication in this life

Many modern scholars, Jewish and Christian, read the Hebrew more narrowly. Job is certain that God (or someone) will clear his name, and he expects to see God while still 'in my flesh'. The book's ending, where God speaks to Job, calls him right and restores him (38:1; 42:5–17), is the fulfillment. On this reading Job's hope is for justice, not for life after death.
Read as a legal hope beyond death

A third group of readers holds that Job expects to die before vindication comes (16:22; 17:1; 19:26), and still believes that his go'el will stand up in court over his dust and that Job himself will see God. How, he does not say. The verse is then a leap of faith beyond what Job or the Old Testament can yet explain, which later revelation filled in.

views.H: Traditional Christian readers take 19:25–27 as a real confession by the historical Job of faith in a living Redeemer and in the resurrection of the body, a faith that God gave him to see ahead of time. Many cite James 5:11 and the Greek ending of the book (42:17), which says Job will rise with those whom the Lord raises.
views.C: Critical scholars generally hold that the Hebrew does not teach bodily resurrection, which is clearly stated only in late texts such as Daniel 12:2. They ask two separate questions. Who is the go'el: God (Gordis, Dhorme), a heavenly advocate distinct from God (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel), or Job's own cry and testimony (Clines)? And when is Job cleared: in this life (Gordis, Dhorme, Clines) or after his death (Pope, Habel)? Most think the vindication Job expects is legal. They also note that 19:26 is one of the hardest lines in the Bible, and that the ancient versions already disagreed.
views.W: Ludlul bel nemeqi, the Babylonian poem of the righteous sufferer, ends with Marduk restoring the sufferer, and it praises Marduk as a god who can bring back the one who has gone down to the grave. The Egyptian Dispute of a Man with His Ba has a man abandoned by brothers and friends, as Job is in 19:13–19. Job's hope differs: it is not a cultic restoration by a city god, but a legal vindication by a living kinsman, which may come after death.
views.J: Jewish commentators mostly read the go'el as God and the passage as Job's hope for justice. The rabbinic Targum keeps 'my redeemer lives' and has 'afterward his redemption will arise upon the dust' and 'from my flesh I will see God again'. Rashi takes the redeemer as God, who lives to avenge Job on his persecutors and will remain when all on earth have perished, and reads 'from my flesh I will see God' as Job seeing God's judgments in his own afflicted body. Ibn Ezra likewise takes 19:26 of the sores God will renew on him. Metzudat David also names God, the eternal one who remains last, and calls the seeing a knowing more certain than bodily sight. The Talmud records the view that Job denied the resurrection of the dead, citing 7:9 (Bava Batra 16a). The Jewish Publication Society translation has 'my Vindicator' and 'while still in my flesh'.
views.X: From 1 Clement 26:3 (about AD 96) on, Christians read 19:25–27 as a prophecy of the resurrection of the body. Jerome wrote, in his treatise against John of Jerusalem (30), that no one since Christ speaks as openly about the resurrection as Job did before Christ, and his Latin made the point sharper than the Hebrew. Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas read the go'el as Christ. The verse is sung in Handel's Messiah and read at Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant funerals.

deep.h: The Hebrew of 19:25–27, line by line
deep.b:
19:25a. 'As for me, I know that my redeemer lives.' The pronoun va'ani, 'as for me', sets Job against the friends who hunt him. Yada'ti, 'I know', is certainty, not wish. Go'ali chai: 'my go'el is alive', the kinsman who rescues, buys back and avenges (see the note).

19:25b. 'At last he will stand up on the dust.' Acharon is 'at last, finally', or a title, 'the Last', or the one who speaks last in court, or the survivor who comes after Job dies. 'Al-'afar is 'on the earth' or 'on the dust' of Job's grave or ash heap. Yaqum is 'he will rise, stand up', the word for a witness taking the stand.

19:26a. 'Even after my skin has been stripped off like this.' The Hebrew is broken: 'and after my skin they have struck off this'. It most likely means that Job's skin will be destroyed, by disease or by death. The KJV's 'worms destroy this body' supplied two words.

19:26b. 'From my flesh I will see God.' 'From my flesh' can mean 'from within my flesh', with a body, or 'apart from my flesh', without one. The grammar allows both, and the whole debate turns here.

19:27. 'I will see him for myself; my own eyes will see, and not a stranger.' Job insists on seeing in person; 'not a stranger' may mean 'not someone else' or 'not as an enemy'. 'My inmost being is spent with longing': literally, 'my kidneys are finished in my bosom'.

deep.h: The Greek, the Latin and the Aramaic
deep.b:
The Greek (Septuagint). The Old Greek reads: 'For I know that everlasting is the one who is about to set me free on the earth, to raise up my skin that endures these things; for these things were accomplished for me by the Lord, which I am conscious of in myself, which my eye has seen and not another, and all have been accomplished for me in my bosom.' The Greek turns 'my redeemer lives' into a statement about God's eternity and makes 'rise' (yaqum) into 'raise up' (anastesai), with Job's skin as the object: a bodily resurrection. The Greek book also ends with a note that Job 'will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up' (42:17).

The Latin (Vulgate). Jerome, translating from the Hebrew in the 390s, wrote: scio enim quod redemptor meus vivat et in novissimo de terra surrecturus sim, et rursum circumdabor pelle mea et in carne mea videbo Deum, 'For I know that my redeemer lives, and on the last (day) I will rise from the earth, and I will be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh I will see God.' The Clementine Vulgate (1592) has 'on the last day', in novissimo die. Jerome makes Job, not the redeemer, the one who rises, and adds the restored skin. These are interpretations, and they shaped the Western church's reading for a thousand years.

The Aramaic (11QtgJob). The Qumran Targum survives in pieces of chapters 17–42. Its columns in this chapter cover about 19:11–19 and resume at 19:29, so 19:20–28 is lost. It cannot tell us how a Jewish translator of the first century BC or AD read the redeemer. The later rabbinic Targum of Job, a different work, survives in full. It stays close to the Hebrew: 'I know that my redeemer lives, and afterward his redemption will arise upon the dust', and 'from my flesh I will see God again'. It does not make Job rise, as the Greek and Latin do.

I checked the Greek in Rahlfs's edition and the NETS translation, the Latin in the Stuttgart (Weber–Gryson) and Clementine texts, and the Aramaic of the rabbinic Targum in the text published on Sefaria, with Mangan's translation as the reference. For 11QtgJob I relied on the published descriptions of its contents. I did not check the Syriac (Peshitta).

deep.h: Four readings, in their strongest form
deep.b:
The readings answer two questions at once, and it helps to keep them apart. Who is the go'el? God, Christ, a heavenly advocate, or Job's own cry. When is Job cleared? In this life, after his death, or at the resurrection. Each reading below is one combination.

1. The resurrection and Christ. The go'el is God, whom Christians know in Christ, and after death and decay Job will see God in his own risen body. In favor: the emphatic 'I know', the language of rising (yaqum) and of seeing God 'from my flesh' with 'my own eyes', after the skin is destroyed; the Greek and Latin translations and almost the whole early church; and the New Testament's teaching that the faithful of old looked for a resurrection (Hebrews 11:13–16, 35). Held by the fathers, Aquinas and Calvin; among modern commentators Francis Andersen argues that the redeemer is God and that Job's hope reaches to resurrection.

2. Vindication within life. The go'el is God, who will defend Job's name before he dies; 'from my flesh' means 'while still in my body'. In favor: Job's hope throughout is for a hearing and a verdict (13:18; 23:3–7; 31:35), the book never otherwise speaks of resurrection, and the ending gives Job exactly this: God appears, speaks, and declares him right (42:5, 7–8). Held by Gordis and Dhorme, and in Jewish tradition by Rashi, who reads 19:26 of Job seeing God's judgments in his body now, and Ibn Ezra.

3. The witness of 16:19. The go'el is the same figure as the witness in heaven: a heavenly advocate who will rise in the divine court to defend Job against God's apparent hostility, even after Job is dead. In favor: the legal words, the link to 9:33, 16:19–21 and 33:23, and the heavenly court of the prologue. Held by Mowinckel; Pope and Habel place the vindication after Job's death, Pope reading 'without my flesh'.

4. Job's own cry. The go'el is no person at all but Job's testimony, the cry for justice he has just wished carved in rock (19:23–24), personified as the witness is in 16:19–20. In favor: the passage moves straight from the written record to the redeemer, and the witness of 16:19 can be read the same way. Clines holds this view, and he distinguishes what Job knows from what he only longs for: to see God for himself, in this life.

The readings overlap. Many Christian readers hold 2 or 3 for the Hebrew and 1 for its fuller meaning: what Job grasped dimly about God as his kinsman is filled out by the resurrection of Christ.

Through the Western church's use of the Latin text, 19:25–27 became one of the best known verses of the Old Testament. The Office of the Dead read Job 19:20–27 at night prayer for the dead, with the responsory Credo quod redemptor meus vivit, 'I believe that my redeemer lives'. The Book of Common Prayer (1549; 1662) begins its burial service with the priest meeting the body and saying 19:25–27 as the procession enters the church. The Catholic funeral lectionary offers Job 19:1, 23–27 as a reading.

Charles Jennens, who compiled the words of Handel's Messiah (1741), opened Part III, on the resurrection, with the KJV of 19:25–26 joined to 1 Corinthians 15:20. The soprano air 'I know that my Redeemer liveth' is one of the most loved pieces of English church music, and Handel's monument in Westminster Abbey shows him holding its score. Hymns such as Samuel Medley's 'I know that my Redeemer lives' (1775) carry the same reading. Through them, many English speakers know the verse in the KJV's words, 'at the latter day' and 'though worms destroy this body', which go beyond the Hebrew.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the go'el answers Bildad's 'no survivor'
deep.b: This is my own reading, offered as a possibility. Bildad's poem ends with the wicked man's line cut off: 'no child or grandchild', 'no one left' (18:19), so there is no one to carry his name or avenge his blood. Job answers point by point in chapter 19: the net (18:8; 19:6), the darkened path (18:6; 19:8), the uprooted tree (18:16; 19:10), the forgotten name (18:17; 19:23–24). The redeemer of 19:25 may answer Bildad's last point. The go'el was exactly the relative who survives a man and acts for him after his death: who buys back his land and avenges his blood (Numbers 35:19; Ruth 4:5, 10). Job's living kin have abandoned him (19:13–19), and his children are dead. So he names a go'el who 'lives' and who will be acharon, 'the one who comes after', the survivor, standing over his dust. Bildad says the wicked have no survivor; Job says that he has one, and that he is alive. The legal-survivor sense of acharon has been proposed by others, and Habel stresses the legal sequence of witness, guarantor and redeemer; the link with 18:19 is my suggestion.

settings.what: Job's reply to Bildad: abandoned by all, he names his living redeemer
settings.to: The three friends (19:2–6, 21–22, 28–29), with the middle of the speech a complaint about God and a cry to anyone who might record it (19:23–24)
settings.when: right after Bildad's portrait of the wicked man trapped and forgotten (18), which Job hears as a portrait of himself
settings.why: Job rejects the friends' inference from suffering to guilt by naming God as the cause (19:6), lays out his total isolation (19:13–19), begs for pity, and then declares his certainty of a living go'el who will vindicate him, ending with a warning that those who judge him will face judgment.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, who had felt abandoned by God and scorned by the nations, Job's certainty that his go'el lives would echo Isaiah's promises that the LORD is Israel's go'el (Isaiah 41:14; Isaiah 43:14; Isaiah 54:5). His wish that his words be written down was granted in this book, which kept his protest and his hope for later sufferers.
views: Job looks to life after death and a bodily seeing of God (the Greek and Latin versions; the church fathers; Andersen).
Job expects God to clear him before he dies, as happens in 42 (Gordis, Dhorme; Rashi).
The go'el is the witness of 16:19, who will defend Job in the heavenly court, perhaps after his death (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel).
The go'el is Job's testimony, personified, which will plead for him (Clines). The chapter page sets out all four.

settings.to: Spoken in the friends' hearing but addressed to no one in particular: a declaration for the record, which Job wishes were carved in rock
settings.when: at the lowest point of his isolation, after listing every relative and friend who has turned away
settings.why: Job puts his testimony on record, so that it will outlast him, and declares that a living kinsman will take his side and that he will see God for himself. The confession is meant to be evidence in the lawsuit he has been building since chapter 9.
settings.readers: The first readers knew the go'el from family law and from the prophets' name for God. Christian readers, from 1 Clement on, heard the risen Christ and the resurrection of the body; Jerome (Against John of Jerusalem 30) said that no one since Christ had spoken as openly of the resurrection as Job did before him. Both kinds of reader find in it a hope that justice will be done even beyond death.

traditions.q: When Job says that after his skin is destroyed he will see God (19:26), does anything of him live on between death and the resurrection?
views: Yes. At death the soul is separated from the body, is judged at once, and lives on; at the last day God gives it back its body, raised and glorified. Job's words, read in the Office of the Dead and the funeral Lectionary, are heard as the hope of the whole person, body and soul.

Yes. The soul lives on after death and already tastes its reward or punishment, and the Church prays for the departed; the full judgment and the raising of the body come at Christ's return. The Greek of 19:26, 'to raise up my skin', is read of that bodily resurrection.

Yes. 'The souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God', while their bodies rest in the grave until the resurrection, when 'the selfsame bodies' are raised. The Westminster Confession lists Job 19:26–27 among its proof texts for that raising (32.2).

No. Death is an unconscious sleep for the whole person until Christ returns; there is no immortal soul that lives on apart from the body. Job's hope is fulfilled only at the resurrection, when he will see God in his own body.
No. The soul is the living person and dies with the body; the dead are unconscious and exist only in God's memory. Job's hope is that God will bring him back to life in the resurrection.

title: The Joy of the Wicked Is Short
sum: Zophar is stung by Job's warning (19:29) and must answer (20:2–3). He does not mention Job's redeemer. Instead he states a truth he says has been known since humans were first put on the earth: the triumph of the wicked is short (20:4–5). Even if his head touches the clouds, the wicked man will vanish like his own dung, fly away like a dream, and his place will not see him again (20:6–9). His sons will repay the poor, and his young strength will lie down with him in the dust (20:10–11).

Then Zophar's great image: evil is sweet food that the wicked man keeps under his tongue, but in his stomach it turns to cobra venom. He vomits up the riches he swallowed, God drives them out of his belly, and he never enjoys the rivers of honey and butter (20:12–18). Because he crushed the poor and grabbed houses, his greed will leave him nothing (20:19–22). As he fills his belly God rains anger on him; he flees an iron weapon and is shot by a bronze bow; darkness, unfanned fire and the testimony of heaven and earth close in on him (20:23–28). 'This is the share God gives a wicked person' (20:29).
readings: Read as a sermon on greed

Zophar's speech is the Bible's most vivid poem on greed. Wealth gained by crushing the poor is sweet in the mouth and poison in the stomach; it cannot be kept, and it turns on its owner. As moral teaching, much of it agrees with the prophets (Micah 2:1–2; Amos 8:4–7) and with Jesus' warning about the rich fool (Luke 12:15–21).
Read as an answer that does not answer

Job has just said he knows his redeemer lives and that he will see God (19:25–27). Zophar ignores it. He answers only Job's warning to the friends (19:29) and returns to his theme. The speech shows how the friends' doctrine has stopped listening: it can only repeat itself, louder.
Read against Job's story

Again the details fit Job: fire from heaven (20:26; 1:16), wealth taken away (20:15, 28; 1:13–17), sons who suffer for their father (20:10). Most pointed of all, heaven and earth will testify against the wicked (20:27), the very witnesses Job called on for himself (16:18–19).

views.H: Traditional readers hear Zophar, the bluntest of the friends, preaching a true sermon to the wrong man. They note that the doctrine he states, the short triumph of the wicked, is taught in Psalm 37 and Psalm 73, and that his mistake is to suppose that Job's suffering proves Job is the greedy oppressor of his poem.
views.C: Critical scholars note the speech's unity: one sustained image of eating and vomiting, poison and food, runs through 20:12–23. Some think that 27:13–23, which opens with nearly the same line as 20:29 (27:13), is a lost third speech of Zophar, since he has none in the third round. The rich vocabulary of food, snakes and weapons is typical of the poet.
views.W: Wisdom texts across the ancient Near East warn that ill-gotten wealth does not last. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope warns against greed and says that riches gained by robbery fly away like geese to the sky. Proverbs 23:4–5, which many scholars think draws on Amenemope, says the same. Zophar's poem belongs to this international wisdom.
views.J: Maimonides assigns Zophar the view of the Ash'ariyya, that everything happens by God's will alone, without a reason humans can know, so that one may not ask why (Guide 3.23).
views.X: Christian preachers have used Zophar's food image as a picture of sin: sweet at first, deadly in the end (Romans 6:23; James 1:14–15). Gregory the Great read the passage morally, of the sinner who enjoys hidden sin. Many Christian commentators, Calvin among them, hold that the friends speak truly of God's judgment in general and wrongly about Job in particular.

deep.b:
Zophar's argument is simple and, in its own terms, strong. It rests on universal experience 'from ancient times' (20:4), on the moral sense that greed is self-destroying, and on God's justice. He does not claim the wicked never prosper; he claims their prosperity is brief and ends in disgrace. The Psalms say the same (Psalm 37:35–36; Psalm 73:18–20).

What Zophar does not do is engage Job. He does not answer Job's claim that God has wronged him (19:6), his list of abandonment (19:13–19), or his confession of a living redeemer (19:25–27). This is Zophar's last speech: in the third round he does not speak at all (unless 27:13–23 is his). His silence after chapter 20 may itself be the poet's comment: the friends' answer has run out.

The Old Greek of chapter 20 is shorter than the Hebrew. It lacked 20:3, 20:9, 20:11 and 20:12–13, and parts of 20:4, 14, 20, 21, 23 and 25; Origen supplied them from Theodotion (I checked the asterisks in NETS). Where it does translate, it often softens or reinterprets: in 20:6 the wicked man's 'gifts' go up to heaven and his 'sacrifice' touches the clouds; in 20:10 'may his inferiors destroy his sons'; in 20:29 God is 'the Overseer' (episkopos). The translator seems to have shortened repeated images and turned some of the poet's hardest pictures into plainer moral statements.

settings.what: Zophar's second speech: the short joy of the wicked
settings.when: immediately after Job's redeemer speech (19), which ended with a warning that the friends who hunt him face judgment
settings.why: Zophar answers the insult he hears in Job's warning (20:2–3) by restating the doctrine: the wicked enjoy their gains only briefly before God makes them disgorge them. He means to show that Job's warning is empty and that judgment falls on the wicked, not on the friends. He says nothing of Job's redeemer.
settings.readers: If the book was read in Persian-period Judah (its date is debated), where wealthy landowners were accused of seizing the houses and fields of the poor (Nehemiah 5:1–13), Zophar's poem was a powerful warning there. Set in Job's story, it also taught them not to assume that every ruined man was such an oppressor.

title: Why Do the Wicked Live On?
sum: Job asks the friends simply to listen; that will be comfort enough (21:2–3). His complaint is with God, so of course he is impatient. Let them look at him and put their hands over their mouths (21:4–6).

Then he answers all three with the facts. The wicked live on, grow old and gain power. Their children are settled around them; their homes are safe; their cattle breed; their children dance to drum and lyre; they die quickly and easily (21:7–13). They tell God to leave them alone and ask what good it does to serve him (21:14–15). How often does their lamp really go out, or disaster come, or the wind blow them away like chaff (21:17–18)? If the friends say God punishes their children, Job answers that the guilty man should pay himself; what does he care about his family after he is dead (21:19–21)?

One man dies at ease, another in bitterness, and the maggots cover both (21:23–26). The friends ask where the tyrant's house is now; Job tells them to ask any traveler, who will tell them that the wicked are spared on the day of disaster, that no one confronts them, and that they are buried with honor and a great procession (21:27–33). So the friends' comfort is empty air, and their answers are faithlessness (21:34).
readings: Read as an argument from experience

Chapter 21 is Job's most direct reply to the friends, and his method is new. They appealed to tradition and to what the fathers taught (8:8–10; 15:18; 20:4). Job appeals to what anyone can see, and what travelers report (21:29). On the evidence, the wicked often prosper to the end. This is the first time in the book that the friends' doctrine is tested against facts.
Read as a protest about justice

Job's point is not that he envies the wicked. He disowns their creed (21:16). His point is that if the wicked go unpunished and the righteous suffer, then the friends' explanation of his suffering collapses, and the question of God's justice is open. That question will be answered, in its own way, by God's speeches (38–41).
Read with Ecclesiastes and Psalm 73

Job's observations are shared by other biblical writers. The psalmist saw the prosperity of the wicked until he went into God's sanctuary and saw their end (Psalm 73). Ecclesiastes saw the wicked buried with honor and one fate for all (Ecclesiastes 8:10; 9:2). Chapter 21 belongs to this honest stream in Scripture.

views.H: Traditional readers see Job, the righteous man, stating hard facts that the friends' theory cannot explain, while keeping himself apart from the wicked (21:16). Christian traditional readers add that the final justice Job does not see in this life is given at the last judgment, so that Job's facts and God's justice are both true.
views.C: Critical scholars note that chapter 21 is the first speech in which Job answers the friends' theme directly, and that it closes the second round with Job's case unanswered. The Old Greek's omission of 21:28–33 is striking. Some see 21:16 and 21:22 as quotations of the friends' views, as 21:19 is, a feature of the book's argumentative style.
views.W: The prosperity of the wicked is the central complaint of the Babylonian Theodicy: the sufferer says that the godless grow rich while he, devout, grows poor, and the friend answers that the gods' ways are remote but the wicked are cut down in the end. In its last stanza the friend admits that the gods gave humans twisted speech, so that people praise the rich and abuse the poor. Job 21 makes the same observation more sharply, and the friends never make the same admission.
views.J: The rabbis took Job's questions seriously. One opinion in the Talmud has Moses ask God why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper (Berakhot 7a). Maimonides reads Job's view in this chapter as close to Aristotle's, that God's providence does not extend to individuals, a view Job will give up after God speaks (Guide 3.23).
views.X: Christian readers have read chapter 21 as proof that justice is not completed in this life, and so as a pointer toward the last judgment and the resurrection: Thomas Aquinas makes this the central argument of the whole debate, with Job holding that reward and punishment are given chiefly after death.

deep.h: Job answers the friends point by point
deep.b:
Chapter 21 picks up the friends' own words and turns them.

The lamp. Bildad: the wicked man's lamp goes out (18:5–6). Job: how often does that happen (21:17)?

Children. Bildad: no child or grandchild (18:19). Zophar: his sons pay for him (20:10). Job: their children are settled around them and dance (21:8, 11); and if God punishes the children instead, that is not justice (21:19–21).

Fear. Eliphaz: the wicked live in dread (15:20–24). Job: their homes are safe from fear (21:9).

Short joy. Zophar: the joy of the wicked lasts a moment (20:5). Job: they spend their days in prosperity and die in an instant, without pain (21:13).

The fallen house. The friends: where is the tyrant's house (21:28; compare 8:22; 15:34; 18:15)? Job: ask the travelers; he is buried in honor (21:29–33).

This is the close of the second round. In the third round (22–27) Eliphaz will drop all hints and accuse Job of specific sins (22:5–9), and the friends' voices will begin to fade.

The Old Greek lacked a large block of this chapter: all of 21:28–33, the travelers' report and the wicked man's honored funeral, as well as 21:15 (the creed of the wicked, 'what is the Almighty?'), 21:21, 21:23 and part of 21:19. Origen supplied them from Theodotion's version and marked them with asterisks; Rahlfs prints them, and NETS marks them. Some scholars think the translator left out lines that he found theologically troubling, such as the wicked man's open defiance and his honored burial; others think he simply shortened a long book, as he did elsewhere. In 21:13, where the Old Greek is present, it reads 'they fell asleep in the rest of Hades', a gentler picture of the wicked man's death.

The Qumran Targum preserves parts of 21:2–10 and 21:20–27 in Aramaic, showing that these verses stood in the Hebrew text it translated.

settings.what: Job's reply to Zophar: the wicked prosper and die in peace
settings.to: The three friends, with a singular 'you' aimed at Zophar in 21:3
settings.when: at the end of the second round, after all three friends have described the fate of the wicked
settings.why: Job answers the friends' shared theme directly, from experience: the wicked often live long, prosper, die easily and are buried with honor, while the good and bad alike end in the dust. His aim is to show that the friends' doctrine cannot explain his suffering, so their comfort is empty and their answers a betrayal.
settings.readers: For Israelites who saw foreign empires and wealthy neighbors prosper while the faithful suffered, Job's honest description gave words to what they saw and refused the easy answer that it could not be so. It left the question for God to answer, as the book's ending does.
